messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mina Tran, a 37-year-old married refugee aid worker, came to treatment after months of feeling as if her life had narrowed around one violent afternoon and the years that followed it. She had been stopped outside a detention center while escorting newly arrived families, when a line of police officers pushed the crowd back without warning. Mina remembered the hard slap of a baton against her arm, the crush of bodies, and the moment she realized the officers were not listening to anyone’s pleas. Even now, when she spoke of it, her face tightened with the same terror she said had hit her in that instant. The memory did not come to her as a distant story; it returned with a vivid force that left her overwhelmed and grieving, as if she were again standing in the press of people and hearing herself think that what had happened was deeply unfair and had never been answered. Since then, certain sights had become potent in ways she found hard to explain to others. When Mina saw a police uniform, a cluster of cyclists weaving through traffic, or a crowded train platform, the jolt of alarm sent her straight back to the afternoon outside the detention center; the scene would flood in before she had time to name what was happening, and she would immediately start scanning for the quickest exit and trying not to think about it. After rare good dinners with her husband, even the feeling of hope itself could make her cut the evening short, because staying with anything that felt too open or too good seemed to invite the next surge of fear. Police uniforms on the street, a cluster of cyclists weaving through traffic near her apartment, or a crowded train platform in the city could send her body into alarm before she had time to reason with herself. In those moments Mina would look for the quickest exit, cut conversations short, and begin trying hard not to think about the trauma. She also avoided situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful; after a rare good dinner with her husband, she would feel a pull to cancel the next outing or not let herself savor the evening, as if joy made her vulnerable. What she feared most was that any one of these cues could open the memory again, and once it came she would have to stop what she was doing because the feelings rose so fast and so high. Mina had come to believe that what happened to her was not only brutal but deeply unfair, and that someone else would not have gotten into this situation. That thought fed her sense that she no longer knew herself; the person who had once been steady in crises now felt unfamiliar to her. It also sharpened her threat monitoring. She found herself watching doorways, scanning faces for authority, and feeling on edge in ordinary settings, especially when the day was busy or unpredictable. At work, where she helped newly resettled families navigate appointments and housing, she began to tense when police were present outside government offices or when a protest passed nearby. The sight of cyclists cutting through a crowded street near the agency could make her stomach drop, and she would move her route or leave early rather than risk the rush of fear that followed. When the memory returned, it did not only bring terror and grief; it also seemed to confirm her beliefs. When the memory broke through, it made the danger feel immediate again, not like something that had ended but like something still pressing in on her body. The same surge of threat made it harder to hold the scene at a distance, so she found herself trying to shut it down, keep busy, or move away from whatever had brought it close. Mina would think, again, that the injustice had never been repaired and that no one had really protected her. Those moments drove her back into suppression, and the more she tried to force the memory away, the more it broke through in sharper form. After a crowded commute or an encounter with police near the shelter where she worked, she would spend the evening replaying fragments of the scene and feeling overwhelmed by emotion, then tell herself that if she could just stay busy enough or shut the whole thing out, she might function. Instead, the strain of holding it down seemed to make the image return with even greater force, and she became more convinced that she was not the person she had been before. To blunt that rising distress, Mina started gambling in the evenings, telling herself she only wanted distraction and a bit of excitement after long days of vigilance. The fact that she had to keep reaching for distraction and risk made her feel, in a quiet and accumulating way, that she could not cope on her own. Over time, the gambling and other ways of staying away from the memory also convinced her that the threat had never really passed, because her body still behaved as if it had to stay one step ahead. After the memory surfaced, she learned that staying in motion, chasing noise, or taking risks could sometimes crowd it out for a while, so the strategies began to follow the memory automatically. The more she depended on them, the more they seemed to leave the event lodged intact and ready to return. She also sought out risky behavior she would once have avoided, taking too many chances in small but worrying ways, as if the adrenaline briefly interrupted the fear. Yet these strategies left her more unsettled. When she lost money or stayed up too late, she felt worse about herself and more certain that something in her had gone wrong. The shame fed her belief that another person would not have ended up like this, and it deepened the sense of identity loss she already carried. It also made her more irritable at home, with angry outbursts that startled her husband and left her feeling even less like herself. Over time, the late-night gambling and constant effort to suppress thoughts made sleep difficult. Mina lay awake listening for sirens, and the exhaustion made the world feel more dangerous the next day. On little sleep she became more reactive, more jumpy around authority figures, and quicker to avoid any place that felt crowded or overfull. What began as an attempt to outrun the trauma had become a life organized around its returns, and she finally sought help when she realized she was pulling away from her husband, her work, and any moment that might bring joy. She is frightened that the memory will keep taking over and that she will keep becoming someone she does not recognize, but she is also hoping that treatment might let her feel safe enough to stay present again. That belief kept pulling her back to the memory, as if she needed to replay the moment to understand how she had ended up there and why it had happened to her. The more she told herself that no one should have had to endure it, the more the scene returned in her mind with vivid force.
